newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan, EU toast broader political ties at summit.
newsitem.headline: Japan, EU toast broader political ties at summit.

text.p: Japan and Europe took a break from their traditional trade bickering on Monday to toast progress towards building a broader common political agenda.
"This was a very successful summit," European Council President John Bruton told a news conference after the fifth annual European Union-Japan summit.
"In earlier meetings the focus was largely on bilateral trade-related issues. On this occasion, we discussed all the outstanding worldwide political problems," said Bruton, the Irish premier.

The global battle against organised crime, United Nations reform, Bosnia, the Middle East peace process, ties with China and Russia, the Korean peninsula and Brussels' relations with Washington were all on the agenda at the talks between a high-level European team and Japanese ministers led by Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto.

"The fifth summit between the European Union and Japan was a clear demonstration that our mutual relationship is becoming strong, intensive and constructive," European Commission President Jacques Santer told the same news conference.
"You see, we covered a whole range of issues," Santer said. "It was not only an economic summit...and that makes a change from the other summits."
The EU has been pressing Japan to take a greater role in international issues.

The latest meeting came against the backdrop of a decline in Europe's trade deficit with Tokyo. The EU has been slowly whittling down the trade gap, which fell to $26 billion last year after soaring to over $40 billion in the late 1980s.
The upbeat tone was doubtless welcomed by Hashimoto, who has called a general election for October 20 and does not need any fresh international problems at the moment.

"The first conclusion (of the summit) was that I was able to establish a personal friendship between myself and Prime Minister Bruton and President Santer," a smiling Hashimoto said in brief remarks after the summit.
Officials said the two sides discussed the EU's financial contribution to KEDO, the international consortium building nuclear power plants in North Korea.
The group, run by the United States, South Korea and Japan, was formed under a 1994 pact in which Washington promised Pyongyang two light-water reactors and interim fuel supplies.
In return, the North pledged to freeze its suspected nuclear weapons programme.

Santer said he hoped EU foreign ministers set to meet in Luxembourg on Tuesday would agree to boost the EU's contribution to KEDO to 15 million Ecus ($12 million) annually for five years in addition to a planned five million Ecus ($4 million) the EU handed over at a Euro-Asian summit in March. In return, the EU wants "adequate representation" on KEDO's executive board.
Trade and investment issues, however, were not neglected.
Besides agreeing to work for a successful World Trade Organisation (WTO) ministerial meeting in Singapore in December, the two sides discussed several bilateral matters.

Among them were foreign access to Japan's insurance market -- the subject of a long-running dispute with the United States -- and what Bruton termed the "general need to continue to press forward with the deregulation and opening of this market for European goods".
